Industry News: Access, Not Chances: How Como Took Manchester United Apart – LC

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game.
  • Industry observers note that cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

Industry observers note that cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

In build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

According to recent reports, close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

Como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

It has been revealed that one detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

It has been revealed that for United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

The decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

According to recent reports, what made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

According to recent reports, A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

It has been revealed that when the build-up ran down the right, it revealed in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

In the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

According to recent reports, especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the newly introduced ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Sources indicate that como bridged the middle third exceptionally swiftly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

Industry observers note that in this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

The connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

Industry observers note that in the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

The intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

Paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

Recent findings suggest that as the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

What carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

Sources indicate that united’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

There were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Recent findings suggest that mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

It has been revealed that on top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

The second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

In a recent development, in the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Industry observers note that como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

The steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

In the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

That isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

Once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

Sources indicate that the double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

It has been revealed that the last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

When Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

In the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

According to recent reports, up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

Sources indicate that the pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

According to recent reports, at half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

The effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

According to recent reports, in the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

Accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

The crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

Tracking the ball for the first goal.

Sources indicate that 1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick promptly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

In a recent development, what follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

The result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

Recent findings suggest that 3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

In a recent development, 4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and shows the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

Como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

Industry observers note that 4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

The common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

Como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

In a recent development, the connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

Industry observers note that for United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

That leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What highlighted regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.

Inter Miami star Lionel Messi was lucky not to have been sent off after hurling the ball in the face of his opponent during an embarrassing MLS Cup Playoff defeat.

In the Round of 16 contest against the Columbus Crew, Miami went down 1-0 early in the first half with a penalty converted by Gonzalo Tapia. The deficit was then compounded when Miami fullback Gonzalo Lujan was sent off with a second yellow card.

On the stroke of halftime, Messi nearly joined his teammate in the locker room with a moment of madness on a throw-in.

Tapia and Messi were both standing out of bounds as the Chilean striker prevented the World Cup winner from taking his throw right away.

Messi then used the ball to shove Tapia's face back. When the Columbus man tried jumping in the air to block the throw, Messi then threw the ball into Tapia's head.

Tapia crumbled to the ground as Messi raised his hands asking for a foul on the Crew star.

Lionel Messi takes a throw-in off Gonzalo Tapia's face pic.twitter.com/jX3tTuojHe.

Lionel Messi nearly got sent off during his team's MLS Cup Playoff match against Columbus.

Recent findings suggest that A frustrated Messi released the ball off the face of Crew striker Gonzalo Tapia as he prevented the Argentina star from taking a quick throw in. Both players received yellow cards.

Tapia got revenge by scoring a brace to lead the Crew to a 3-0 victory on Saturday evening.

Referee Allen Chapman was not happy with either player's antics, showing yellow cards to both Tapia and Messi.

But ultimately, Columbus and Tapia would get the last laugh as they won 3-0 in the best-of-three Round of 16.

Midfielder Taha Habroune scored the second goal of the evening in the 52nd minute as Tapia secured a brace just six minutes later.

The result has Inter Miami on the brink of elimination from the playoffs after winning the title last season. Columbus dominated every facet of the game, thanks in part to owning 62 percent of possession.

Messi attempted two shots on the evening – counting for half of the saves from Crew keeper Patrick Schulte.

Inter Miami must win the next match in Ohio to stay in the playoffs. If the game finishes tied, the rules dictate the match will proceed directly to penalty kicks.

Out of his three prior seasons in the United States, Messi's 2025 MLS Cup victory was an outlier. Miami missed the playoffs in 2023 and were eliminated in the first round in 2024.

L'Union rapporte les propos de l'entraîneur rémois Nicolas Usaï après la première défaite à domicile de la saison de son équipe, désormais à 10 longueurs de ses bourreaux d'hier, les solides leaders stéphanois.

"Il y a de la déception par rapport à l’engagement que l’on a mis dans le match. On sait que ça se joue sur des détails, on a concédé peu d’occasions par rapport à la faculté de notre adversaire. On n’a pas été assez efficaces dans nos moments forts, particulièrement dans les 25 premières minutes. Après le but, on a manqué un peu d’allant, peut-être un peu d’énergie. On savait que c’était une opposition de qualité. Rien à reprocher aux joueurs dans le comportement, dans l’engagement.

La maîtrise était stéphanoise. Dans le coeur du jeu, ils ont réussi à éteindre rapidement les quelques étincelles que l’on a pu avoir. On est déçus par rapport au résultat. Quand on joue dans un stade comme ça, avec de nombreux supporters, on a envie de pouvoir communier avec eux à la fin et ce n’est pas le cas. Par rapport au peu d’occasions que l’on a subies, c’est très frustrant.

Industry observers note that saint-Étienne fait un écart, Nancy a encore gagné, Montpellier avait perdu, c’était l’occasion de repasser devant... On est à la 13e journée et au-delà du classement, il faut être lucide par rapport à ce ce que l’on est en capacité de faire, même s’il faut rester mesuré, ne pas être alarmiste. Là, la défaite à Grenoble fait encore plus mal.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.
  • In a recent development, city face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League.
  • If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules. It is a decision that, if upheld, would equate to one of the biggest scandals in football history.

In a recent development, city face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League. Or a combination of all, under rule W51 of its handbook. No punishment has yet been confirmed.

If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.

Recent findings suggest that the charges can be broken down into five categories and relate to a period from 2009-23 in which City won six League Cups, three FA Cups, seven league titles and the Champions League. There is the provision for removing past titles, but that would appear remote.

City have been the dominant force in English football for most of that time, but that status is under threat with a verdict that will send shockwaves around Europe and could have huge ramifications for the club.

That is unless they can win an appeal, with sources cautioning it still may take up to another two to three years for the case to be resolved, following on from an already five-year investigation.

The Premier League’s rules provide for an independent appeal board with broad powers, including the ability to uphold, vary or overturn the independent commission’s decision.

It would therefore appear that despite the verdict, the case is far from being resolved and punishment decided. The details of the commission’s findings, when published, will be crucial to determining what happens next.

But if it is upheld, the verdict also opens up the possibility of City facing legal action from other clubs who feel they missed out on trophies and even merit money from league placings.

It is understood Premier League clubs are already discussing legal action and possible compensation claims as a result of the guilty verdict.

Each of those cases would have to be held individually, potentially leading to years more of litigation. Conversely, if City win their appeal, they too could take legal action against the Premier League the damage caused to their reputation.

Recent findings suggest that there has not yet been an official confirmation of the independent panel’s verdict from the Premier League. The Premier League declined to comment.

However, several sources have told Telegraph Sport that the panel has found City guilty of all but one of the charges they faced. The one that has not been proved is stated to be one of the most serious of the 115.

Recent findings suggest that the damning verdict for City is a major new test of fragile UK relations with the United Arab Emirates, with whom bilateral trade was worth £25bn last year. Redacted freedom of information documents, seen by Telegraph Sport, show Abu Dhabi hosted UK government officials including Lord Stockwood, then investment minister, as recently as February. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the City chairman and trusted adviser to the UAE president, was present at the meeting. Government notes from the meeting recorded that he “noted they are very proud of what they have achieved through their investments in Manchester”.

The Government previously caused acrimony among senior leaders in Abu Dhabi after putting forward legislation to ban foreign states from owning UK newspapers and news magazines. The intervention prompted the collapse of a takeover of The Telegraph in April 2024, which was largely funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the owner of City and vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

Recent findings suggest that the previous UK government has admitted its embassy in Abu Dhabi and the Foreign Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) in London discussed the charges levelled at City by the Premier League. However it refused to disclose the correspondence.

Recent findings suggest that city have steadfastly maintained they are innocent, promising “irrefutable” evidence in support of their position, and had assembled some of the most expensive lawyers in the country to argue their case. Despite the verdict, the club are understood to be confident that it will win the argument in the end. Senior figures are said to be calm about the latest development, as significant as it seems.

In a recent development, city rebuilt their team this summer and it is understood that signings were brought in on conventional player contracts, rather than terms including clauses triggered in the event of a heavy punishment. Given the club have consistently denied breaching financial regulations, and their deals for newly introduced players to work with head coach Enzo Maresca underlines their position.

According to recent reports, on Friday, a City spokesman said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”.

Sources close to Pep Guardiola, the former City manager who stepped down last summer after 10 years of remarkable success at the club, including a treble triumph in 2023 and an unprecedented fourth straight league title in 2024, insist he has not been informed of any verdict.

In the days after City were first charged, Guardiola mounted a fierce defence of the club, claiming: “I am fully convinced we will be [proved] innocent.”.

The verdict vindicates the Premier League’s decision to launch an investigation after explosive allegations that City had routinely broken financial rules were first made in Der Spiegel in 2018 based on the Football Leaks documents.

Uefa previously accused City of breaches of its financial regulations and announced in 2020 that it was suspending the club from the Champions League for two years for “overstating” sponsorship revenue between 2012 and 2016.

According to recent reports, city denied the Uefa charges and, after an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the two-year ban was overturned. Cas found that a number of the claims brought by Uefa had fallen outside a five-year “time bar” and others were “not established”.

It has been revealed that it did, however, still impose a €10m fine after ruling that City failed to cooperate with investigators. City had previously also agreed a settlement with Uefa of €20m in 2014 following an investigation into their finances.

It has been revealed that legal experts agreed that the commission’s verdict is far from the end of the case. Yasin Patel, barrister at Church Court Chambers, said: “City’s lawyers will now analyse this decision and look at the options open to them to appeal, which may include procedural impropriety, wrongful interpretation of law, and legal errors – importantly, they can guarantee an appeal.

Sources indicate that “Sanctions could include a major fine, points deduction, relegation or even all three. Factoring in whether titles and trophies should be stripped, whether other clubs have been robbed of further revenue and opportunities due to City’s wrongdoings and losses incurred, we safely say that this is only the first chapter of a long-running legal saga that will not end any time soon.”.

Sources indicate that ian Hargreaves, partner with specialist disputes firm Quillon Law, stated the verdict was “not the end of the story but the beginning of a new phase”, and added: “There is also the question of whether the panel’s decision can withstand a hard-fought appeal, and on what grounds any challenge might be brought. Much will depend on the detail of the panel’s findings and reasoning, which will inevitably be closely scrutinised by both sides.”.

Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri, who won the Ballon d’Or during his trophy-laden spell at the club, said he believed the club were innocent.

Recent findings suggest that “For the players, it’s different than it is for journalists. I can understand all opinions, but we try to stay positive,” the Spain midfielder noted while on international duty.

According to recent reports, “When you see all the people who worked hard at City to achieve success, you know what we achieved can’t be taken away. It wasn’t paid for with money, but with effort and teamwork. Everything we achieved was deserved; we marked one of the great eras of English football. I believe in the club’s innocence – we already went through this in 2020.”.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, mentioned: “I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”.

Zohran Kwame Mamdani, the mayor of Upcoming York, posted “114” in relation to the charges while former Manchester United players David de Gea and Rio Ferdinand both asked whether they should be due winner’s medals from past seasons.

According to recent reports, the Premier League statement in February 2023 said that “a number of alleged breaches” had been referred to an independent commission. It then detailed each specific rule against each season in which the alleged breach took place. The precise number was not clear from the statement and led to varying reports between 115 and 130. Friday’s news suggested the figure was 115.

Industry observers note that all the way to 2009-10, the first full season following the club’s takeover by Sheikh Mansour, who is a member of the Abu Dhabi Royal family and the vice president of the United Arab Emirates. There were charges relating to all 14 seasons until the Premier League completed their investigation during the 2022-23 campaign. In that time, City won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Champions League. They have since won another league title – the first club to do so four times in a row – as well as the Uefa Super Cup, the Fifa Club World Cup and the FA Cup and League Cup double last season.

Recent findings suggest that they can be split into five groups. The biggest relates to the seasons from 2009-10 until 2017-18 and the requirement for clubs to provide accurate financial information and act in the utmost good faith.

The next set of rules concern the full disclosure of manager and player payments. The alleged manager breaches related to the period between 2009-10 and 2012-13, when Roberto Mancini was leading the team. The alleged breaches with respect to player payments relate to all of the seasons between 2010-11 and 2015-16.

Industry observers note that as well as providing financial detail, clubs were required to meet Uefa and Premier League rules which were designed to bring a club’s spending broadly in line with their income by placing set limits on losses. City were charged with breaches of Uefa’s licencing and financial fair play rules from 2013-14 until 2017-18, and the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules from 2015-16 until 2017-18.

The final set of charges spanned the five seasons during which City were being investigated by the Premier League and rules that require members to cooperate in the utmost good faith by providing information and documents.

A full picture will only emerge when the commission publishes its findings but we know that the Premier League investigation began in December 2018 following allegations in the German newspaper Der Spiegel based on the Football Leaks documents. These included alleged payments to former manager Mancini for consultancy work at an Abu Dhabi-based club that was separate to his regular contract at City.

It has been revealed that we also know that City were alleged to have breached rules over setting out image rights payments to players in their club contract. Der Spiegel reported that the Premier League investigation also focused on payments to under-age players, as well as whether club sponsors were paying for commercial deals themselves or a significant proportion was in fact effectively coming from owner Sheikh Mansour.

City have always denied breaking any rules. In response to the Premier League statement about the alleged breaches, they mentioned that they have “irrefutable evidence” to support their position and “look forward to this matter being put to rest once and for all.”.

In a recent development, at the start of the hearing in September 2024, Guardiola also said: “Wait for the independent panel. We believe we have not done anything wrong.”.

Industry observers note that of the Football Leaks documents, City said: “We will not be providing any comment on out-of-context materials. The attempt to damage the club’s reputation is organised and clear.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dans sa dernière édition, L'Union revient sur la déplorable absence des supporters stéphanois dans le parcage du stade Auguste-Delaune. Extraits.

Recent findings suggest that "Selon nos informations, un nouvel encadrement des supporters stéphanois a été créé par les autorités le matin même du match. Des autobus neutres accueillis à un péage sur le parcours et escortés jusqu'au stade. C'est d'ailleurs pour cela qu'ils sont partis. Le parcage d'Auguste-Delaune, de nouveau ouvert, et le Stade de Reims, étaient de nouveau prêts à les faire venir. Et ce, quelques heures avant le coup d'envoi du match. Sauf que la préfecture de la Marne, que nous avons contactée, ne l'a pas entendu de cette oreille et maintient : tout transport véhiculant des Stéphanois entrant dans le département sera intercepté et le parcage visiteur reste fermé.

Mais l'information n'a pas le temps de circuler. Le Stade de Reims l'apprend au dernier moment, pareil pour les supporters stéphanois déjà partis en bus. Certains rebroussent chemin, d'autres persistent. Ce qui donne une scène assez folle au péage de Champfleury, au sud de la Cité des Sacres. Les bus et minibus sont arrêtés par les forces de l'ordre et sommés de retourner d'où ils viennent. Près de 6 heures pour l'aller et la même chose pour le retour. Pour ces supporters, la rencontre se regardera sur la route... Cruel.

It has been revealed that ce qui n'est pas le cas d'autres, plus malins, qui avaient pris leur ticket dans d'autres tribunes, notamment tout proche du parcage resté vide. Munis d'ailleurs sous leur blouson de maillot et d'écharpe aux couleurs de l'ASSE, jusque-là bien cachés, mais qui ont été ressortis au coup d'envoi. Ceux-là, plusieurs centaines, ont pu donner de la voix, surtout après la victoire de leur club. Mais l'ambiance aurait pu prendre plus d'ampleur avec la présence de leurs partenaires. C'est quand même mieux un stade garni...".

Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb.

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

Recent findings suggest that “We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

“Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

However, the goal that would have made the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager’s debut as an international boss more memorable ultimately failed to arrive.

In this extended international break, the Scots will host Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday and then travel to North Macedonia before taking on Slovenia in Glasgow, with the Tartan Army hoping to see further improvement – and goals.

September 29: Scotland vs Switzerland.

October 3: North Macedonia vs Scotland.

October 6: Scotland vs Slovenia.

November 13: Scotland vs North Macedonia.

November 16: Switzerland vs Scotland.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, the debutant said: “Thought we struggled to get into the game first half, but second half we completely dominated the game.

According to recent reports, “They’ve got a top goalie who made really good saves. So many positives to take and a clean sheet as well.

“We changed shape a wee bit at half-time to get more control and that did really well for us.

“It’s a significant game again on Tuesday so it’s vital to recover now and go again.

“I’ve played on the left-hand side for a couple of years now, so I’m comfortable doing that.

Sources indicate that “We’ve had a great week. A fresh manager, new way of playing and new faces in camp. It’s just the chances we need to take - the fact we’re creating the chances stands us in good stead.”.

The striker told BBC Scotland: “It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play.

Sources indicate that “We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored.

Industry observers note that “I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

In a recent development, “Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

It has been revealed that pocognoli’s first game in charge of Scotland ends in a goalless draw. The visitors produced a dominant second-half display, but their final ball and end-product was severely lacking in crucial moments. Ure, Hickey, Gilmour, McBurnie and Bowie all came close to scoring, but no one could break the deadlock.

Scotland cannot find a way past the impenetrable Oblak. There will be just two minutes of added time for the visitors to possibly score a late winner.

Lovric clatters into Gilmour and is cautioned. Slovenia can’t get out. It’s wave after wave of Scottish pressure.

According to recent reports, oblak comes out and fails to claim Robertson’s free-kick. The ball is recycled and the Tottenham full-back whips a second cross into the box and Slovenia fail to clear. Welsh is waiting for it, but lashes a first-time volley over the bar.

Karnicnik catches Robertson with a late lunging tackle and receives a yellow card, giving Scotland a chance to get the ball into the box.

The hosts make their fifth alteration of the afternoon, with Cerin withdrawn and Lovric on instead.

Industry observers note that how has Bowie missed?! Gilmour finds Bowie with an outstanding pass through the centre of Slovenia’s defence. The substitute takes a touch then scuffs a rushed finish wide. Bowie has to do better there!

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Pocognoli’s Scotland finished the half as the better side, but an opening goal has proved to be elusive. At times, they’ve looked suspect defensively and have lacked rhythm going forward. However, Pocognoli’s squad have only been together for a few days and are playing in a new system. Can they produce a more inspired second-half performance?

Matko goes on the outside of Welsh, and from a tight angle, he shoots, but his fizzed effort saves the side netting of the near post. Some fans behind the goal cheer because they think it’s gone in, but their view has really deceived them.

It’s been a quiet afternoon for both goalkeepers so far, with neither yet to make a noteworthy save. On a couple of occasions, Slovenia have had encouraging opportunities to get the ball into the Scotland’s box, but the deliveries have been overhit and poorly executed.

Similarly to Scotland, Slovenia are also playing a tremendously high-line. Unlike Slovenia, Scotland have been unable to find the right pass in behind the home side’s defence. Gilmour then carelessly gives the ball away as Scotland’s latest spell of possession ends.

The hosts get us underway in the Slovenian capital. Can Pocognoli begin his Scotland tenure with a Nations League victory?

According to recent reports, “I hope we can bring a good game, and a good exciting principle on the pitch. I think we need the support from the supporters because there’s a lot of newly introduced players.

“We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

Scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his new role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 01:42 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 05:02 EST, 23 November 2026.
  • Given the carousel of chaos and never-ending crises at Old Trafford, it is easy to forget there are football storylines away from the headline-generating machine of Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino.
  • Lo and behold, there is – and Liverpool also enter Sunday’s clash against the old enemy with a point to prove.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 01:42 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 05:02 EST, 23 November 2026.

Given the carousel of chaos and never-ending crises at Old Trafford, it is easy to forget there are football storylines away from the headline-generating machine of Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino.

Lo and behold, there is – and Liverpool also enter Sunday’s clash against the old enemy with a point to prove.

One problem for Andoni Iraola is his side's frailties in the bigger games, which comes into focus this weekend with United in town – despite the desire to make an easy joke about how this is a clash against relegation fodder.

Since thrashing United 7-0 in 2023, Liverpool have beaten their friends in Manchester just once in seven meetings, including two draws and a defeat at Anfield.

It has been revealed that to use a cliche, form seems to go out of the window for this fixture. In the last two Anfield meetings, Liverpool have been first and second in the table, United 14th and then tenth. This weekend, it is fourth against 18th, though Pochettino’s side could be bottom by kick-off.

Liverpool’s struggles in bigger games stretch further. Against the so-called 'Big Six’, the Reds have won just two of 12 games since winning the Premier League title. In a ‘mini league’ of those six sides, Liverpool are bottom in the aforementioned period.

Andoni Iraola's Liverpool side must prove on Sunday they can deliver in the biggest matches.

Manchester United did the double over Liverpool in the Premier League last season.

United did the double over Liverpool last season, Manchester City have beaten them four times in little over 12 months, Arsenal won on Merseyside a month ago.

Recent findings suggest that so why has this team gone from looking formidable 18 months ago to rather flappable whenever the historic significant boys are in town? Casual neutrals who only tune in for the showpiece Sunday 4.30pm may joke that they have not seen Liverpool play well for a good year.

A lot of the answer to that question comes back to Arne Slot and the challenges we documented every week last season, when his side were dull and boring to watch, naked in defence and would capitulate in an instant.

Maybe players like Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola thrive more in intricate spaces rather than the gaping gaps left behind by the attack-minded bigger teams.

Another reason could be the simple fact that these sides are more likely to expose Liverpool’s vulnerabilities, such as the lack of a true defensive midfielder, the poor full backs or the frailties at defending set-pieces.

According to recent reports, anfield has lost its fear factor somewhat, too. Liverpool are top of the Premier League away table with 13 points from 15, but 18th in the home table with just one win in five games.

Sources indicate that city had not won in front of a crowd there since 2003, now they have done it two seasons running. Arsenal had not triumphed at the stadium for 14 years until last month.

In a recent development, iraola is aware of all this and said on Friday: ‘United finished third in the table last season. You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season.

Liverpool bemoaned Ryan Gravenberch’s red card in their home defeat to Manchester City.

The Reds spurned a number of chances when they were beaten 1-0 by Arsenal last month.

‘Now we have just started, this is just 10 games. So, for sure, they will be a lot higher in the table (soon). We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third.

According to recent reports, ‘We have to look at ourselves because we need the points. We need to improve our home form. It is also a big game in terms of relevance. It’s Liverpool v Manchester United, so we want to play well and we want to win.’.

In a recent development, asked if he understands the importance of the fixture to fans, Iraola – who spent the weekend off taking in grassroots football and netball games following his kids – said: ‘I am very aware! This is the biggest one in English football. In this country, this is the one.’.

According to recent reports, in Iraola’s first two bigger games, a theme threatened to emerge. Against Manchester City, Liverpool were well in the contest until Ryan Gravenberch’s red card but were toothless when it came to putting their chances away, lacking bite in attack.

The game was there to be won at 0-0, with the Anfield crowd roaring, but the Reds did not have the killer instinct to do so.

In a recent development, against Arsenal, there were plenty of chances to equalise after the Gunners’ early goal but, again, goalkeeper David Raya could have put his feet up and had a cigar. A lot of territory but nothing to make the defence seriously sweat.

In a recent development, in both cases, Liverpool were on the receiving end of refereeing howlers. Gravenberch’s red was not a red – the first yellow should never be a booking – and Alexander Isak had a stonewall penalty turned down. ProRef has admitted errors.

It has been revealed that to take a cynical view, though: in the title-winning campaign, we were rarely sat talking about referees or moaning about narrow misses or unfair results. Liverpool found ways to win and had no excuses.

Liverpool need Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak to step up against the league's substantial boys.

And that brings us nicely on to Sunday. It feels like the script has been written for weeks.

Indeed, after United lost 3-0 to Bournemouth and the score was read out to huge cheers at Anfield, Daily Mail Sport wrote: ‘Everyone is looking forward to United sacking Michael Carrick and then rocking up at Anfield to win 1-0 with their latest manager in a few weeks.’.

It always seems to happen and it feels like United get results against rivals Liverpool and City even when they have felt close to their lowest ebb.

Sources indicate that but Liverpool and Iraola must not allow that to happen. There can be no excuses of ‘new manager bounce’, refereeing calls or fine margins come Sunday tea time.

Isak and Wirtz simply must step up. It feels harsh that the pair, Wirtz especially, are always in the spotlight but the £125million and £116million signings have flattered to deceive against the big boys.

Both have been spectacular at times this term but need to show up when it really matters, while £123million addition Barcola is still waiting for his first Premier League goal.

Iraola has history with United. As a player, his Athletic Club side beat Sir Alex Ferguson’s great side 5-3 over two legs in Europe.

‘I said at the time, it was one of the best wins of my career,’ he said. 'United, I remember, were champions of the Premier League, got to the Champions League final and lost to Barcelona the year before. We honestly played much better than them.’.

Iraola has remained unbeaten against United into his managerial career, winning two and drawing four of his six meetings with them.

Overall, the former Bournemouth boss has played 38 games against ‘Big Six’ teams in the league: winning ten, drawing ten, losing 18.

But a win is all that matters on Sunday and it is a chance for Liverpool to set the tempo ahead of a busy festive schedule. After already taking on the current top three, Iraola now contests two rivalries with a trip across the city to Everton next week.

Six of nine pre-Christmas games are at Anfield so there is a real chance to build a head of steam in the league, qualify for the next stage of Europe and get to the Carabao Cup semi-final.

Iraola would welcome those festive gifts but, for Liverpool fans, nothing will be sweeter than giving their old foes a good old walloping on Sunday.

Mais ce match permet aux jeunes de rester dans le rythme, il permet aussi de donner du temps de jeu à ceux qui en avaient moins et d'intégrer les joueurs revenant de blessure".
